lesson.title: Multiplexing the Web: How HTTP/2 Ended the Waterfall
lesson.summary: HTTP/2 keeps the same request and response model as HTTP/1.1 but changes how requests travel over the wire, using a binary framing layer to run many requests at once over a single connection.
lesson.body:
HTTP/1.1 has a structural problem that becomes obvious once a page needs dozens of resources. Each connection can only carry one request at a time; the response has to come back before the next request on that same connection can start. This is called head of line blocking. Browsers worked around it by opening several TCP connections to the same server, typically around six, so multiple requests could be in flight at once. That workaround costs something too: every TCP connection needs its own handshake, and browsers still had to ration those six connections across dozens or hundreds of resources on a modern page, which produces the familiar staggered, waterfall style loading pattern.

HTTP/2 solves this at the application layer without changing what a request or response means. It introduces a binary framing layer underneath the familiar HTTP semantics: methods, headers, status codes, and bodies all still exist, but instead of being sent as readable text, they are broken into small binary frames, each tagged with a stream identifier. Many streams can share a single TCP connection, and their frames can be interleaved on the wire in any order and reassembled by stream ID on the other end. A client can open a request for the HTML document, the stylesheet, and a dozen images all at once, on one connection, without waiting for any of them to finish first.

HTTP/2 also compresses headers using a scheme called HPACK, which matters because HTTP/1.1 requests repeat a lot of the same header fields, like cookies and user agent strings, on every single request. HPACK lets both sides maintain a shared table of previously seen header fields and send small references to it instead of the full text each time, shrinking the overhead of chatty request patterns.

It is important to be precise about what problem this actually fixes. HTTP/2 eliminates head of line blocking at the HTTP layer, the browser no longer has to wait for one response to finish before starting the next. But all of those multiplexed streams are still riding on a single TCP connection, and TCP guarantees in order delivery of bytes. If one TCP segment is lost anywhere in that stream of interleaved frames, TCP will not hand any of the bytes after it to the application, including bytes that belong to completely unrelated HTTP/2 streams, until the lost segment is retransmitted and arrives. So a single dropped packet can stall every in flight request on the connection even though, from HTTP's point of view, those requests are independent. This gap between what HTTP/2 fixed and what it could not fix, because the head of line blocking has simply moved down to the transport layer, is exactly the motivation for the next major step in HTTP's evolution.
